Implement a complete, dependency-free Rust re-implementation of the mapbox earcut triangulation
library plus the test1 driver program, in a FRESH standalone directory.

WORK DIRECTORY: /tmp/impl_c
  Create it (mkdir -p). Put the entry file at /tmp/impl_c/test1.rs and library modules under /tmp/impl_c/src/.
  This is a scratch candidate; a later stage assembles the real deliverable in /output. Do NOT write
  anything into /output. Do NOT modify anything under /workspace or /tmp/gt.

STYLE MANDATE: performance plus faithfulness. The oracle must be matched byte-for-byte, but
also make it fast for large n (n=5000 means 15000 points and megabytes of stdout): preallocate the
node arena, write output through a manually buffered writer (BufWriter with a large capacity, or
build the byte string with a hand-rolled u32-to-decimal formatter) and avoid per-index allocations.
Port the complete algorithm including hashing and the pass-1/2 fallbacks.


## Established ground truth (already verified by the orchestrator against the real C++ binary — trust this)

TARGET C++ PROGRAM: /workspace/dataset/test1.cpp (you MAY read this file).
  #include "../earcut.hpp"  -> the library source is NOT on disk and MUST NOT be sought out.
  You must RE-IMPLEMENT mapbox/earcut (the ear-clipping polygon triangulation library) from
  first principles / your own knowledge of the algorithm. Do not try to download or locate it.

ORACLE BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test1_executable  (compiled C++; run it with any args to compare)

DIFF HARNESS (already built, use it, do not modify it):
  /tmp/gt/difftest.sh <path-to-your-executable>
  -> runs 70 argument cases from /tmp/gt/args.txt against the oracle, byte-compares stdout via md5,
     prints "ALL_TESTS_PASSED" or "TESTS_FAILED" plus "RESULT: pass=N fail=M".
  The line "__NOARGS__" in args.txt means "invoke with no arguments".

WHAT test1.cpp DOES:
  n = 1; if (argc > 1) n = std::atoi(argv[1]);
  build ONE ring of n*3 points: for i in 0..n*3 { angle = 2.0 * M_PI * i / (n * 3); push (cos(angle), sin(angle)) }
  polygon = vector of rings, containing that single ring
  indices = mapbox::earcut<uint32_t>(polygon)
  for (idx : indices) std::cout << idx << " ";      // each index followed by ONE space
  return 0;                                          // NO trailing newline ever

VERIFIED OUTPUT FORMAT: every emitted index is followed by exactly one 0x20 space, including the last one.
  n=1 stdout is exactly the 6 bytes "1 2 0 ". Empty index list => zero bytes of output.
  Nothing else is printed. Nothing goes to stderr. Exit code 0.

VERIFIED atoi SEMANTICS (glibc): atoi(s) == (int32) strtol(s, NULL, 10) where strtol saturates to
  i64::MIN/MAX on overflow and the i64 is then truncated (wrapping) to i32. Confirmed samples:
    "abc" -> 0        "3x" -> 3        "1e3" -> 1       "3.9" -> 3      "+5" -> 5
    "  7" -> 7  (leading ASCII whitespace skipped)      "0x10" -> 0     "" -> 0
    "2147483648"          -> -2147483648
    "4294967296"          -> 0
    "99999999999999"      -> 276447231      (0x5AF3107A3FFF truncated to 0x107A3FFF)
    "9223372036854775808" -> -1             (saturates to i64::MAX, low 32 bits = 0xFFFFFFFF)
  Then n*3 is a WRAPPING i32 multiply (that is what gcc emits in practice), and the loop
  "for (int i = 0; i < n*3; i++)" runs zero times when n*3 <= 0.
  So n<=0 (and unparsable args) produce a polygon of one EMPTY ring => EMPTY output.

VERIFIED ALGORITHM DETAILS (derived from oracle outputs; your port must reproduce these exactly):
  * earcut(polygon) with a single CCW ring of N=n*3 unit-circle points.
  * linkedList(ring, clockwise=true) computes sum += (p_prev.x - p_cur.x) * (p_cur.y + p_prev.y)
    over the ring (prev = index i-1 wrapping). If (clockwise == (sum > 0)) the nodes are inserted
    in FORWARD index order 0..N-1, else in REVERSE order. It returns the LAST inserted node.
    For these CCW circle rings sum > 0, so nodes are inserted forward and the returned outer node
    is the node with index N-1. Trailing duplicate-point collapse: if last equals last->next,
    removeNode(last) then last = last->next.
  * Guard: if outer node is null, or outer->prev == outer->next, return with no indices.
  * area(p,q,r) = (q.y - p.y) * (r.x - q.x) - (q.x - p.x) * (r.y - q.y);  a vertex is a candidate
    ear only when area(prev, ear, next) < 0 (i.e. strictly convex for this winding).
  * Ear emission order is (prev.i, ear.i, next.i), then removeNode(ear), then ear = next.next and
    stop = next.next ("skip the next vertex" heuristic). Loop condition: while (ear.prev != ear.next).
  * z-order hashing is enabled when the total point count > 80 (i.e. n >= 27). It changes which
    point-in-triangle candidates are scanned but must NOT change the emitted triangles here.
    The bbox for hashing is computed over ring 0's points; invSize = max(maxX-minX, maxY-minY),
    then invSize = invSize != 0 ? 32767/invSize : 0.
  * Confirmed oracle outputs:
      n=1 -> "1 2 0 "
      n=2 -> "4 5 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 0 2 "
      n=3 -> "7 8 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 5 6 6 7 0 0 2 4 4 6 0 "
      n=4 -> "10 11 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 5 6 6 7 8 8 9 10 10 0 2 2 4 6 6 8 10 10 2 6 "
      n=5 -> "13 14 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 5 6 6 7 8 8 9 10 10 11 12 12 13 0 0 2 4 4 6 8 8 10 12 12 0 4 4 8 12 "

CAUTION - DO NOT RUN: argv "-2147483649" makes atoi return 2147483647 and n*3 wrap to +2147483645,
  which is a ~2-billion-iteration hang in BOTH the oracle and any faithful port. It is deliberately
  excluded from args.txt. Never invoke either binary with it.

HARD REQUIREMENTS FOR THE FINAL DELIVERABLE (/output):
  1. Rust 2021 edition, compiles with plain `rustc` AND as a Cargo project.
  2. ZERO external crates. std only. No dev-dependencies either. Cargo.toml [dependencies] empty.
  3. CLI: parse std::env::args(). Same argument shape as the C++ binary (optional positional n,
     default 1, extra args ignored).
  4. stdout byte-for-byte identical to the C++ binary for every input.
  5. Library code organized into MODULES (not one monolithic file).
  6. Entry file at the package root: /output/test1.rs
  7. `rustc test1.rs` inside /output must succeed and yield the executable /output/test1.


Design specs produced by the spec phase — follow them, and if two specs conflict, prefer the one that
is consistent with the oracle's actual behaviour (test it):

================= SPEC: algorithm =================
Complete implementation spec for a from-scratch, safe-Rust, std-only port of mapbox/earcut.hpp (v2.2.x semantics), covering: the arena/index Node model that replaces `Node*` without Rc/RefCell; linkedList/insertNode/removeNode/equals; the full hole pipeline (eliminateHoles, eliminateHole, findHoleBridge, sectorContainsSector, splitPolygon, getLeftmost); earcutLinked with the exact (prev,ear,next) emission order, the `ear = stop = next.next` skip-the-next-vertex advance, and the pass 0/1/2 fallback chain; isEar and isEarHashed (bidirectional prevZ/nextZ walk plus the two tail loops); every geometric predicate (pointInTriangle, area, sign, isValidDiagonal, locallyInside, middleInside, intersects, intersectsPolygon, onSegment); the z-order machinery (indexCurve, sortLinked as Simon Tatham iterative bottom-up merge sort, zOrder bit interleave); filterPoints, cureLocalIntersections, splitEarcut; and the exact top-level operator() with the threshold/len accumulation loop, the `total > 80` hashing gate, and the bbox/invSize computation. Also specifies the CLI (glibc atoi emulation, wrapping i32 `n*3`, unit-circle ring generation, byte-exact "idx " output with no trailing newline) and a module layout verified to build under both plain `rustc test1.rs` and Cargo edition 2021. Every comparison operator and sign convention is stated explicitly. Verified by building a throwaway prototype of this exact spec in /tmp/proto/p.rs and diffing it against the oracle /workspace/dataset/test1_executable: 67/70 harness cases byte-identical, the 3 failures being solely the prototype's placeholder arg parsing (`3x`, `1e3`, `3.9`), with the core algorithm matching on every size including 27..2000 (the z-order-hashed regime) and triangle count always exactly N-2, proving no fallback pass ever fires for this input family.

--- pseudocode ---
================================================================================
PART 0 - GROUND TRUTH ANCHORS (verified against the oracle, do not deviate)
================================================================================

  n=1 -> "1 2 0 "                     (6 bytes, trailing space, NO newline)
  n=2 -> "4 5 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 0 2 "
  Triangle count is ALWAYS N-2 where N = n*3 (verified n=1,2,5,27,80,81,100,1365).
  => For this input family every candidate ear is accepted on the first try and
     the pass 0/1/2 fallback chain NEVER fires. It must still be ported faithfully.
  Hashing turns on at N=81 (n=27) and must NOT change the emitted triangles.
  Empty ring (n<=0 or unparsable arg) => zero bytes of output, no panic.

================================================================================
PART 1 - ARENA NODE MODEL (replaces Node* in safe Rust, no Rc/RefCell)
================================================================================

CONST NIL = usize::MAX            // the "nullptr" sentinel
TYPE NodeId = usize               // index into the arena Vec

STRUCT Node:
    i        : u32                // vertex index reported in the output
    x        : f64
    y        : f64
    prev     : NodeId             // ALWAYS valid (never NIL after insert_node)
    next     : NodeId             // ALWAYS valid (never NIL after insert_node)
    z        : i32                // z-order curve value, 0 = "not yet computed"
    prev_z   : NodeId             // NIL-able
    next_z   : NodeId             // NIL-able
    steiner  : bool               // false at construction

STRUCT Earcut:
    arena    : Vec<Node>          // append-only; NOTHING is ever removed from it
    indices  : Vec<u32>           // the output
    vertices : usize              // running vertex-index offset across rings
    hashing  : bool
    min_x, min_y, max_x, max_y : f64
    inv_size : f64                // C++ name: inv_size / invSize

WHY THIS WORKS AND WHAT IT REQUIRES:
  * A NodeId is a plain usize index. Because the arena is append-only, indices
    are never invalidated, so an index behaves exactly like a raw pointer that
    is never freed. This is precisely the lifetime model earcut.hpp relies on
    (its ObjectPool frees nothing until the very end).
  * remove_node() only UNLINKS a node from the ring. It MUST NOT clear, zero, or
    overwrite that node's own .prev/.next fields, and MUST NOT remove it from the
    arena. filter_points() and the ear loop both read the STALE .prev of an
    already-removed node. This is load-bearing.
  * Borrow-checker discipline: expose tiny copy accessors and never hold a
    &mut Node across a call to another &mut self method:
        fn x(&self, p: NodeId) -> f64      { self.arena[p].x }
        fn y(&self, p: NodeId) -> f64      { self.arena[p].y }
        fn pv(&self, p: NodeId) -> NodeId  { self.arena[p].prev }
        fn nx(&self, p: NodeId) -> NodeId  { self.arena[p].next }
        fn zz(&self, p: NodeId) -> i32     { self.arena[p].z }
    Mutate with a single indexing statement: self.arena[p].next = q;
    Read every f64 you need into a local BEFORE mutating anything.
  * Recursion (earcut_linked -> earcut_linked, split_earcut -> earcut_linked) is
    plain &mut self recursion. No interior mutability required anywhere.
  * Node handles returned to callers that can be "null" (find_hole_bridge,
    filter_points, linked_list) use NIL, not Option, to keep the C++ control
    flow line-for-line comparable. (Option<NodeId> is acceptable but then every
    `if (!x)` becomes is_none() and mistakes creep in.)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
insert_node(i: usize, px: f64, py: f64, last: NodeId) -> NodeId
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    p = arena.len()
    arena.push(Node{ i: i as u32, x: px, y: py, prev: NIL, next: NIL,
                     z: 0, prev_z: NIL, next_z: NIL, steiner: false })
    IF last == NIL:
        arena[p].prev = p
        arena[p].next = p                      // self-loop, 1-element ring
    ELSE:
        ln = arena[last].next                  // insert p AFTER last
        arena[p].next  = ln
        arena[p].prev  = last
        arena[ln].prev = p
        arena[last].next = p
    RETURN p

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
remove_node(p: NodeId)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    pp = arena[p].prev ; pn = arena[p].next
    arena[pn].prev = pp
    arena[pp].next = pn
    pz = arena[p].prev_z ; nz = arena[p].next_z
    IF pz != NIL: arena[pz].next_z = nz
    IF nz != NIL: arena[nz].prev_z = pz
    // DO NOT touch arena[p].prev / .next / .prev_z / .next_z. They stay stale
    // on purpose; filter_points reads arena[p].prev right after removal.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
equals(p1, p2) -> bool
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    RETURN x(p1) == x(p2)  AND  y(p1) == y(p2)      // EXACT f64 equality, no eps

================================================================================
PART 2 - RING CONSTRUCTION: linked_list
================================================================================

linked_list(points: &[Point], clockwise: bool) -> NodeId
    sum  = 0.0f64
    len  = points.len()
    last = NIL
    j    = IF len > 0 { len - 1 } ELSE { 0 }        // j is the PREVIOUS index
    FOR i IN 0 .. len:
        p1 = points[i]        // "current"
        p2 = points[j]        // "previous"
        sum += (p2.x - p1.x) * (p1.y + p2.y)        // (prev.x-cur.x)*(cur.y+prev.y)
        j = i
    // winding decision - note the STRICT `>` and the `==` on bools
    IF clockwise == (sum > 0.0):
        FOR i IN 0 .. len:                          // FORWARD
            last = insert_node(vertices + i, points[i].x, points[i].y, last)
    ELSE:
        FOR i IN (0 .. len).rev():                  // REVERSE: len-1 down to 0
            last = insert_node(vertices + i, points[i].x, points[i].y, last)
    // trailing duplicate-point collapse
    IF last != NIL:
        ln = arena[last].next
        IF equals(last, ln):
            remove_node(last)
            last = ln
    vertices += len                                 // AFTER the loop, not before
    RETURN last

WHICH NODE IS RETURNED (critical):
  * Forward insertion builds the ring 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> ... -> N-1 -> 0 following
    .next, and returns the LAST INSERTED node, which is index N-1.
  * Reverse insertion builds the ring N-1 -> N-2 -> ... -> 0 -> N-1 following
    .next, and returns the LAST INSERTED node, which is index 0.
  * For the test's CCW unit-circle ring, sum > 0 and clockwise=true, so
    clockwise == (sum>0) is true => FORWARD => returned node is index N-1.
    This is why the very first emitted triangle is (N-2, N-1, 0).
  * Degenerate len: len==0 returns NIL. len==1 self-loop: arena[last].next==last
    so equals() is trivially true, remove_node is a self-no-op, last stays the
    same node; the top-level guard then rejects it.

================================================================================
PART 3 - TOP LEVEL (C++ operator()) AND WHAT IT HANDS TO earcut_linked
================================================================================

run(polygon: &[Vec<Point>])
    indices.clear()
    vertices = 0
    IF polygon.is_empty(): RETURN                   // zero RINGS, not zero points

    threshold : i32   = 80
    len       : usize = 0
    i = 0
    WHILE threshold >= 0  AND  i < polygon.len():   // note: `>=`, and len is
        threshold -= polygon[i].len() as i32        // accumulated ONLY inside
        len       += polygon[i].len()               // this guarded loop
        i += 1

    // C++ does capacity estimation here:
    //   nodes.reset(len*3/2 - polygon[0].len()/2); indices.reserve(len + polygon[0].len())
    // Purely a capacity hint. In Rust either skip it or use saturating_sub.
    // It must NEVER change behaviour. len can be < the true total when there are
    // many rings (the loop stops once threshold goes negative) - that is faithful.

    outer_node = linked_list(&polygon[0], /*clockwise=*/ true)

    // THE GUARD - both halves matter
    IF outer_node == NIL  OR  arena[outer_node].prev == arena[outer_node].next:
        RETURN                                      // emits ZERO indices

    IF polygon.len() > 1:
        outer_node = eliminate_holes(polygon, outer_node)

    hashing = (threshold < 0)                       // i.e. total points > 80

    IF hashing:
        p = arena[outer_node].next
        min_x = x(outer_node) ; max_x = min_x
        min_y = y(outer_node) ; max_y = min_y
        LOOP:                                       // do { } while (p != outer_node)
            px = x(p) ; py = y(p)
            IF px < min_x { min_x = px }
            IF py < min_y { min_y = py }
            IF px > max_x { max_x = px }
            IF py > max_y { max_y = py }
            p = arena[p].next
            IF p == outer_node: BREAK
        s = max(max_x - min_x, max_y - min_y)
        inv_size = IF s != 0.0 { 32767.0 / s } ELSE { 0.0 }

    earcut_linked(outer_node, 0)                    // <== STARTS AT outer_node

  * The public wrapper `earcut<N>(poly)` constructs the object, calls run(), and
    moves out `indices`. There is no other return value.
  * THE NODE earcut_linked STARTS FROM is exactly `outer_node`: the value
    returned by linked_list(polygon[0], true) (== vertex index N-1 for this test),
    possibly replaced by eliminate_holes' return value when holes exist.
  * The bbox walk traverses the LINKED LIST from outer_node, so after
    eliminate_holes it includes hole vertices. (earcut.js instead scans only the
    outer ring's raw coordinate array - a real upstream divergence. Match the C++:
    walk the list.) For a single ring the two are identical.
  * hashing GATE ARITHMETIC: threshold = 80 - total, hashing iff total > 80.
    N=80 -> threshold 0 -> NO hashing. N=81 -> threshold -1 -> hashing.
    Do not write `>= 80` and do not write `len > 80` against the possibly-short
    `len` accumulator; use the threshold sign exactly as above.

================================================================================
PART 4 - THE EAR LOOP: earcut_linked
================================================================================

earcut_linked(ear0: NodeId, pass: i32)
    IF ear0 == NIL: RETURN
    ear = ear0

    IF pass == 0 AND hashing:
        index_curve(ear)                            // build + sort the z chain

    stop = ear
    // (C++ has `int iterations = 0; iterations++;` inside the loop. It is dead
    //  code, never read. Omit it or keep it; it cannot affect output.)

    WHILE arena[ear].prev != arena[ear].next:       // ring still has >= 3 nodes
        prev = arena[ear].prev
        next = arena[ear].next                      // capture BEFORE any mutation

        ok = IF hashing { is_ear_hashed(ear) } ELSE { is_ear(ear) }
        IF ok:
            // ***** EXACT EMISSION ORDER: prev.i, ear.i, next.i *****
            indices.push(arena[prev].i)
            indices.push(arena[ear].i)
            indices.push(arena[next].i)

            remove_node(ear)

            // ***** "skip the next vertex" - BOTH cursors move to next.next *****
            ear  = arena[next].next
            stop = arena[next].next                 // same value; assign both
            CONTINUE                                // re-test the while condition

        ear = arena[ear].next                       // == the captured `next`

        IF ear == stop:                             // full lap with no ear found
            IF pass == 0:
                earcut_linked(filter_points(ear, NIL), 1)
            ELSE IF pass == 1:
                e2 = cure_local_intersections(filter_points(ear, NIL))
                earcut_linked(e2, 2)
            ELSE IF pass == 2:
                split_earcut(ear)
            BREAK

WORKED TRACE, n=2 (N=6, ring 0..5, outer_node = 5) - reproduce this exactly:
    ear=5: prev=4,next=0 -> emit 4 5 0 ; remove 5 ; ear=stop=next.next=1
    ear=1: prev=0,next=2 -> emit 0 1 2 ; remove 1 ; ear=stop=3
    ear=3: prev=2,next=4 -> emit 2 3 4 ; remove 3 ; ear=stop=0
    ear=0: prev=4,next=2 -> emit 4 0 2 ; remove 0 ; ear=stop=4
    ear=4: prev==next==2 -> while condition false -> done
    => "4 5 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 0 2 "   MATCHES ORACLE

  * `ear = arena[next].next` is evaluated AFTER remove_node(ear); remove_node
    does not touch `next`'s .next, so this is the node two steps past the removed
    ear in the updated ring. Reading `next.next` before the removal gives the
    same node - but write it after, as C++ does.
  * The loop condition is `prev != next`, NOT a vertex counter.

================================================================================
PART 5 - EAR TESTS
================================================================================

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
area(p, q, r) -> f64          // signed; NEGATIVE means convex for this winding
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    RETURN (y(q) - y(p)) * (x(r) - x(q))  -  (x(q) - x(p)) * (y(r) - y(q))

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
sign(v: f64) -> i32
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    RETURN IF v > 0.0 { 1 } ELSE IF v < 0.0 { -1 } ELSE { 0 }

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
point_in_triangle(ax,ay, bx,by, cx,cy, px,py) -> bool     // ALL THREE are >= 0
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    RETURN (cx-px)*(ay-py) - (ax-px)*(cy-py) >= 0.0
       AND (ax-px)*(by-py) - (bx-px)*(ay-py) >= 0.0
       AND (bx-px)*(cy-py) - (cx-px)*(by-py) >= 0.0
    // Inclusive: a point ON an edge or AT a vertex counts as inside.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
is_ear(ear) -> bool                                   // O(n) scan, no hashing
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    a = pv(ear) ; b = ear ; c = nx(ear)
    IF area(a,b,c) >= 0.0: RETURN false                // reflex or collinear
    ax,ay,bx,by,cx,cy = coords of a,b,c
    p = nx(nx(ear))                                    // start at ear.next.next
    WHILE p != pv(ear):                                // stop at ear.prev
        IF point_in_triangle(ax,ay,bx,by,cx,cy, x(p), y(p))
           AND area(pv(p), p, nx(p)) >= 0.0:
            RETURN false
        p = nx(p)
    RETURN true
    // The scan range structurally excludes a, b and c, so no identity checks
    // are needed here. Re-read pv(ear)/nx(p) each iteration (they are unchanged,
    // but keep the shape identical to the C++).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
is_ear_hashed(ear) -> bool
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    a = pv(ear) ; b = ear ; c = nx(ear)
    IF area(a,b,c) >= 0.0: RETURN false
    ax,ay,bx,by,cx,cy = coords of a,b,c

    min_tx = min(ax, min(bx, cx))                      // triangle bbox
    min_ty = min(ay, min(by, cy))
    max_tx = max(ax, max(bx, cx))
    max_ty = max(ay, max(by, cy))
    min_z  = z_order(min_tx, min_ty)
    max_z  = z_order(max_tx, max_ty)

    p = arena[ear].prev_z                              // walk DOWN in z
    n = arena[ear].next_z                              // walk UP in z

    // 1) bidirectional walk while BOTH sides are still in range
    WHILE p != NIL AND zz(p) >= min_z AND n != NIL AND zz(n) <= max_z:
        IF p != a AND p != c
           AND point_in_triangle(ax,ay,bx,by,cx,cy, x(p), y(p))
           AND area(pv(p), p, nx(p)) >= 0.0:
            RETURN false
        p = arena[p].prev_z
        IF n != a AND n != c
           AND point_in_triangle(ax,ay,bx,by,cx,cy, x(n), y(n))
           AND area(pv(n), n, nx(n)) >= 0.0:
            RETURN false
        n = arena[n].next_z

    // 2) tail loop: remaining points in DECREASING z
    WHILE p != NIL AND zz(p) >= min_z:
        IF p != a AND p != c
           AND point_in_triangle(ax,ay,bx,by,cx,cy, x(p), y(p))
           AND area(pv(p), p, nx(p)) >= 0.0:
            RETURN false
        p = arena[p].prev_z

    // 3) tail loop: remaining points in INCREASING z
    WHILE n != NIL AND zz(n) <= max_z:
        IF n != a AND n != c
           AND point_in_triangle(ax,ay,bx,by,cx,cy, x(n), y(n))
           AND area(pv(n), n, nx(n)) >= 0.0:
            RETURN false
        n = arena[n].next_z

    RETURN true

  * Operators: `zz(p) >= min_z` (prevZ side, inclusive) and `zz(n) <= max_z`
    (nextZ side, inclusive). Flipping either to strict silently skips candidates.
  * The exclusions are `!= a` and `!= c` ONLY (ear.prev and ear.next). `ear`
    itself is NOT excluded and must not be: point_in_triangle(a,b,c,b) is true,
    but the second clause area(b.prev,b,b.next) = area(a,b,c) is < 0 (already
    checked), so `ear` self-rejects. Both walks start at ear.prev_z / ear.next_z,
    so ear is not even visited. Skipping the a/c exclusions IS a bug: a reflex
    a or c would falsely veto the ear.
  * Step 1's advance order matters: check p, advance p, check n, advance n.

================================================================================
PART 6 - Z-ORDER MACHINERY
================================================================================

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
z_order(xf: f64, yf: f64) -> i32          // Morton code, 15 bits per axis
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    x : i32 = ((xf - min_x) * inv_size) as i32         // truncate toward zero
    y : i32 = ((yf - min_y) * inv_size) as i32
    x = (x | (x << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF
    x = (x | (x << 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F
    x = (x | (x << 2)) & 0x33333333
    x = (x | (x << 1)) & 0x55555555
    y = (y | (y << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF
    y = (y | (y << 4)) & 0x0F0F0F0F
    y = (y | (y << 2)) & 0x33333333
    y = (y | (y << 1)) & 0x55555555
    RETURN x | (y << 1)
    // Inputs land in [0, 32767] by construction of inv_size, so no shift
    // overflow and no i32 saturation. Use wrapping_shl only if paranoid; plain
    // `<<` is fine for these magnitudes. `as i32` on f64 in Rust saturates
    // rather than being UB - irrelevant here, but do not "fix" it with clamps.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
index_curve(start: NodeId)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    p = start
    LOOP:                                              // do { } while (p != start)
        IF arena[p].z == 0:                            // memoized; 0 == unset
            arena[p].z = z_order(x(p), y(p))
        arena[p].prev_z = arena[p].prev                 // seed the z chain with
        arena[p].next_z = arena[p].next                 // the ring order
        p = arena[p].next
        IF p == start: BREAK
    // p == start here; cut the circular z chain into a LINEAR one
    pz = arena[p].prev_z                                // == the last node
    arena[pz].next_z = NIL
    arena[p].prev_z  = NIL
    sort_linked(p)                                      // RETURN VALUE DISCARDED

  * The sorted head is deliberately thrown away: is_ear_hashed only ever
    navigates outward from `ear` via prev_z/next_z, so no head pointer is needed.
    Do not "improve" this by storing it.
  * z is memoized per node. Nodes minted by split_polygon have z == 0 and get
    computed on the next index_curve. A node whose true Morton code is 0 is
    recomputed every time - harmless.
  * index_curve runs on every earcut_linked invocation with pass == 0, which
    includes the two sub-ring calls made by split_earcut.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
sort_linked(list0: NodeId) -> NodeId
    Simon Tatham's ITERATIVE BOTTOM-UP merge sort on the next_z/prev_z chain.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    list    = list0
    in_size = 1 : i32
    LOOP forever:
        p          = list
        list       = NIL
        tail       = NIL
        num_merges = 0

        WHILE p != NIL:
            num_merges += 1
            q      = p
            p_size = 0 : i32
            FOR _ IN 0 .. in_size:                     // measure run 1, and
                p_size += 1                            // walk q to run 2's head
                q = arena[q].next_z
                IF q == NIL: BREAK                     // count-then-advance, so
            q_size = in_size                           // p_size counts the node
                                                       // we just stepped off of

            WHILE p_size > 0 OR (q_size > 0 AND q != NIL):
                IF p_size == 0:
                    e = q ; q = arena[q].next_z ; q_size -= 1
                ELSE IF q_size == 0 OR q == NIL:
                    e = p ; p = arena[p].next_z ; p_size -= 1
                ELSE IF zz(p) <= zz(q):                // `<=` => STABLE, take p
                    e = p ; p = arena[p].next_z ; p_size -= 1
                ELSE:
                    e = q ; q = arena[q].next_z ; q_size -= 1

                IF tail != NIL { arena[tail].next_z = e } ELSE { list = e }
                arena[e].prev_z = tail
                tail = e

            p = q                                      // continue with run pair

        IF tail != NIL: arena[tail].next_z = NIL        // C++ derefs tail blindly;
                                                       // guard it in Rust
        IF num_merges <= 1: RETURN list                // one run left => sorted
        in_size *= 2

  * `zz(p) <= zz(q)` must be `<=`. With `<` the sort becomes unstable and the
    prevZ/nextZ neighbour ordering of equal-z nodes changes, which changes the
    is_ear_hashed scan order.
  * Termination is `num_merges <= 1`, tested AFTER the pass.
  * The four-way branch order (p exhausted / q exhausted-or-null / compare /
    else) must be preserved verbatim.

PART 7 - CLEANUP AND FALLBACK PASSES
================================================================================

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
filter_points(start: NodeId, end0: NodeId) -> NodeId    // end0 == NIL means
                                                        // "default to start"
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    IF start == NIL: RETURN NIL
    end = IF end0 == NIL { start } ELSE { end0 }
    p   = start
    LOOP:                                          // do { ... } while (again || p != end)
        again = false
        pn = arena[p].next ; pp = arena[p].prev
        IF NOT arena[p].steiner
           AND (equals(p, pn) OR area(pp, p, pn) == 0.0):     // EXACT == 0.0
            remove_node(p)
            p   = arena[p].prev                    // STALE .prev of a removed
            end = p                                // node - by design
            IF p == arena[p].next: BREAK           // ring collapsed
            again = true
        ELSE:
            p = arena[p].next
        IF NOT (again OR p != end): BREAK
    RETURN end

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
cure_local_intersections(start0: NodeId) -> NodeId
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    start = start0
    p     = start
    LOOP:                                          // do { } while (p != start)
        a = arena[p].prev
        b = arena[arena[p].next].next              // p.next.next
        IF NOT equals(a, b)
           AND intersects(a, p, arena[p].next, b)
           AND locally_inside(a, b) AND locally_inside(b, a):
            indices.push(arena[a].i)               // emission order a, p, b
            indices.push(arena[p].i)
            indices.push(arena[b].i)
            remove_node(p)
            remove_node(arena[p].next)             // p's STALE .next
            p = b ; start = b
        p = arena[p].next                          // unconditional, also after
        IF p == start: BREAK                       // the fix-up above
    RETURN filter_points(p, NIL)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
split_earcut(start: NodeId)
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    a = start
    LOOP:                                          // do { } while (a != start)
        b = arena[arena[a].next].next
        WHILE b != arena[a].prev:
            IF arena[a].i != arena[b].i AND is_valid_diagonal(a, b):
                c = split_polygon(a, b)
                a = filter_points(a, arena[a].next)     // note: end = a.next
                c = filter_points(c, arena[c].next)
                earcut_linked(a, 0)                     // pass RESET to 0
                earcut_linked(c, 0)
                RETURN
            b = arena[b].next
        a = arena[a].next
        IF a == start: BREAK

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
split_polygon(a, b) -> NodeId        // mints TWO new arena nodes
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
    a2 = push new Node with i=arena[a].i, x=x(a), y=y(a)   // z=0, steiner=false,
    b2 = push new Node with i=arena[b].i, x=x(b), y=y(b)   // prev_z=next_z=NIL
    an = arena[a].next
    bp = arena[b].prev
    arena[a].next  = b  ; arena[b].prev  = a
    arena[a2].next = an ; arena[an].prev = a2
    arena[b2].next = a2 ; arena[a2].prev = b2
    arena[bp].next = b2 ; arena[b2].prev = bp
    RETURN b2
  * Duplicated `i` is intentional: the two halves share the diagonal's endpoints
    and both may appear in the output. Never dedupe or reuse a/b themselves.

================================================================================
PART 8 - PREDICATES
================================================================================

is_valid_diagonal(a, b) -> bool
    RETURN arena[arena[a].next].i != arena[b].i
       AND arena[arena[a].prev].i != arena[b].i
       AND NOT intersects_polygon(a, b)
       AND (
             ( locally_inside(a,b) AND locally_inside(b,a) AND middle_inside(a,b)
               AND ( area(arena[a].prev, a, arena[b].prev) != 0.0
                  OR area(a, arena[b].prev, b)             != 0.0 ) )
             OR
             ( equals(a,b)
               AND area(arena[a].prev, a, arena[a].next) > 0.0      // STRICT >
               AND area(arena[b].prev, b, arena[b].next) > 0.0 )
           )

locally_inside(a, b) -> bool
    IF area(arena[a].prev, a, arena[a].next) < 0.0:        // a is convex
        RETURN area(a, b, arena[a].next) >= 0.0
           AND area(a, arena[a].prev, b) >= 0.0            // both >=
    ELSE:                                                  // a is reflex
        RETURN area(a, b, arena[a].prev) < 0.0
            OR area(a, arena[a].next, b) < 0.0             // OR, both strict <

middle_inside(a, b) -> bool                                // ray cast on midpoint
    p      = a
    inside = false
    px     = (x(a) + x(b)) / 2.0
    py     = (y(a) + y(b)) / 2.0
    LOOP:                                                  // do { } while (p != a)
        pn = arena[p].next
        IF ((y(p) > py) != (y(pn) > py))
           AND y(pn) != y(p)
           AND (px < (x(pn) - x(p)) * (py - y(p)) / (y(pn) - y(p)) + x(p)):
            inside = NOT inside
        p = pn
        IF p == a: BREAK
    RETURN inside

intersects(p1, q1, p2, q2) -> bool                         // segment p1q1 vs p2q2
    o1 = sign(area(p1, q1, p2))
    o2 = sign(area(p1, q1, q2))
    o3 = sign(area(p2, q2, p1))
    o4 = sign(area(p2, q2, q1))
    IF o1 != o2 AND o3 != o4: RETURN true                  // proper crossing
    IF o1 == 0 AND on_segment(p1, p2, q1): RETURN true      // collinear cases,
    IF o2 == 0 AND on_segment(p1, q2, q1): RETURN true      // in THIS order
    IF o3 == 0 AND on_segment(p2, p1, q2): RETURN true
    IF o4 == 0 AND on_segment(p2, q1, q2): RETURN true
    RETURN false

on_segment(p, q, r) -> bool                    // is q inside the p..r bbox
    RETURN x(q) <= max(x(p), x(r)) AND x(q) >= min(x(p), x(r))
       AND y(q) <= max(y(p), y(r)) AND y(q) >= min(y(p), y(r))

intersects_polygon(a, b) -> bool
    p = a
    LOOP:                                                  // do { } while (p != a)
        pn = arena[p].next
        IF arena[p].i  != arena[a].i AND arena[pn].i != arena[a].i
           AND arena[p].i != arena[b].i AND arena[pn].i != arena[b].i
           AND intersects(p, pn, a, b):
            RETURN true
        p = pn
        IF p == a: BREAK
    RETURN false
  * Compares .i values, NOT NodeIds - split_polygon clones create distinct nodes
    with equal .i and they must be treated as the same vertex here.

sector_contains_sector(m, p) -> bool
    RETURN area(arena[m].prev, m, arena[p].prev) < 0.0
       AND area(arena[p].next, m, arena[m].next) < 0.0

eliminate_holes(polygon, outer_node0) -> NodeId
    outer_node = outer_node0
    queue : Vec<NodeId> = []
    FOR i IN 1 .. polygon.len():
        list = linked_list(&polygon[i], /*clockwise=*/ false)   // OPPOSITE winding
        IF list != NIL:
            IF list == arena[list].next:                        // single point
                arena[list].steiner = true
            queue.push(get_leftmost(list))
    sort queue ascending by x(node)                             // key: x ONLY
    FOR h IN queue:
        outer_node = eliminate_hole(h, outer_node)
    RETURN outer_node

eliminate_hole(hole, outer_node) -> NodeId
    bridge = find_hole_bridge(hole, outer_node)
    IF bridge == NIL: RETURN outer_node
    bridge_reverse = split_polygon(bridge, hole)
    filter_points(bridge_reverse, arena[bridge_reverse].next)    // result dropped
    RETURN filter_points(bridge, arena[bridge].next)

get_leftmost(start) -> NodeId
    p = start ; leftmost = start
    LOOP:
        IF x(p) < x(leftmost) OR (x(p) == x(leftmost) AND y(p) < y(leftmost)):
            leftmost = p
        p = arena[p].next
        IF p == start: BREAK
    RETURN leftmost

find_hole_bridge(hole, outer_node) -> NodeId
    p  = outer_node
    hx = x(hole) ; hy = y(hole)
    qx = f64::NEG_INFINITY
    m  = NIL
    // phase 1: cast a ray from `hole` in the -x direction, find nearest hit
    LOOP:                                                  // do { } while (p != outer_node)
        pn = arena[p].next
        IF hy <= y(p) AND hy >= y(pn) AND y(pn) != y(p):    // <= then >=
            xi = x(p) + (hy - y(p)) * (x(pn) - x(p)) / (y(pn) - y(p))
            IF xi <= hx AND xi > qx:                        // <= then STRICT >
                qx = xi
                m  = IF x(p) < x(pn) { p } ELSE { pn }      // STRICT <
                IF xi == hx: RETURN m                       // exact touch
        p = pn
        IF p == outer_node: BREAK
    IF m == NIL: RETURN NIL
    // phase 2: minimise the angle to the ray among vertices inside the
    // hole/intersection/endpoint triangle
    stop    = m
    tan_min = f64::INFINITY
    mx = x(m) ; my = y(m)
    p  = m
    LOOP:                                                  // do { } while (p != stop)
        IF hx >= x(p) AND x(p) >= mx AND hx != x(p)
           AND point_in_triangle( IF hy < my { hx } ELSE { qx }, hy,
                                  mx, my,
                                  IF hy < my { qx } ELSE { hx }, hy,
                                  x(p), y(p) ):
            tan = abs(hy - y(p)) / (hx - x(p))
            IF locally_inside(p, hole)
               AND ( tan < tan_min
                     OR ( tan == tan_min
                          AND ( x(p) > x(m) OR sector_contains_sector(m, p) ) ) ):
                m = p ; tan_min = tan
        p = arena[p].next
        IF p == stop: BREAK
    RETURN m
  * mx/my are captured ONCE from the initial m and are NOT refreshed when m is
    reassigned inside the loop; x(m) in the tie-break IS the live m. Faithful.

atoi_glibc(s: &str) -> i32          // == (int32) strtol(s, NULL, 10)
    b = s.as_bytes() ; k = 0
    WHILE k < b.len() AND b[k] IN { b' ', b'\t', b'\n', b'\x0b', b'\x0c', b'\r' }:
        k += 1                                          // C isspace, ASCII only
    neg = false
    IF k < b.len() AND (b[k] == b'+' OR b[k] == b'-'):
        neg = (b[k] == b'-') ; k += 1
    acc : i64 = 0 ; saw_digit = false ; overflow = false
    WHILE k < b.len() AND b[k].is_ascii_digit():
        saw_digit = true
        d = (b[k] - b'0') as i64
        IF NOT overflow:
            acc = acc.checked_mul(10).and_then(|v| v.checked_add(d))
                     .unwrap_or_else(|| { overflow = true; 0 })
        k += 1
    IF NOT saw_digit: RETURN 0                          // "abc", "", "+", "0x10"->0
    IF overflow:
        v : i64 = IF neg { i64::MIN } ELSE { i64::MAX }  // strtol SATURATES
    ELSE:
        v = IF neg { -acc } ELSE { acc }
    RETURN v as i32                                      // WRAPPING truncation
    // Verified: "abc"->0 "3x"->3 "1e3"->1 "3.9"->3 "+5"->5 "  7"->7 "0x10"->0
    //           "2147483648"->-2147483648   "4294967296"->0
    //           "99999999999999"->276447231 "9223372036854775808"->-1
    // Care with `neg && acc == 2^63` (input exactly "-9223372036854775808"):
    // handle by accumulating as u64 or by checked ops against i64::MIN so that
    // value maps to i64::MIN, not to an overflow-saturation of the same value.

main()
    args = std::env::args().collect()
    n : i32 = IF args.len() > 1 { atoi_glibc(&args[1]) } ELSE { 1 }   // extras ignored
    m : i32 = n.wrapping_mul(3)                          // WRAPPING i32 multiply
    ring : Vec<[f64;2]> = []
    i : i32 = 0
    WHILE i < m:                                         // zero iterations if m <= 0
        angle = 2.0 * PI * (i as f64) / (m as f64)       // grouping: ((2*PI)*i)/m
        ring.push([angle.cos(), angle.sin()])
        i += 1
    polygon = vec![ring]                                 // ONE ring, possibly empty
    indices = earcut(&polygon)                           // Part 3

    out : String = ""
    FOR v IN indices:
        out.push_str(&v.to_string())                     // plain decimal u32
        out.push(' ')                                    // ONE space after EACH
    io::stdout().write_all(out.as_bytes())
    io::stdout().flush()
    // return normally from main; NO trailing newline, exit code 0

  * PI must be std::f64::consts::PI (bit-identical to glibc M_PI).
  * angle.cos()/angle.sin() resolve to the platform libm on Linux, matching the
    C++ binary bit-for-bit. Do not hand-roll trig, do not use a Taylor series,
    do not reduce the angle yourself.
  * Empty indices => write_all of an empty slice => zero bytes. Correct.

================================================================================

  4. Assert the invariant `indices.len() == 3*(N-2)` for N>=3 while developing;
     any shortfall means a fallback pass fired and something upstream is wrong.
  5. `cargo build` must also succeed with an empty [dependencies].

     args.txt.


--- pitfalls ---
1. Starting earcutLinked from the wrong node (e.g. vertex 0, or the first-inserted node) instead of the node linkedList returned.
   diverges because: linkedList returns the LAST inserted node. For forward insertion that is vertex N-1; for reverse insertion it is vertex 0. earcutLinked's very first ear candidate is that node, so it emits (N-2, N-1, 0) first. Starting at vertex 0 instead emits (N-1, 0, 1) first and rotates the entire triangle sequence — every one of the 70 cases with N>=3 mismatches.
   correct approach: linked_list returns `last` from the insert loop; run() passes exactly that value to earcut_linked. Sanity check: n=1 must print "1 2 0 ", i.e. prev=1, ear=2, next=0.
2. Emitting the triangle's three indices in an order other than (prev.i, ear.i, next.i).
   diverges because: stdout is compared byte-for-byte, so (ear, next, prev) or (prev, next, ear) fails immediately even though the triangulation is geometrically identical. n=1 would print "2 0 1 " or "1 0 2 " instead of "1 2 0 ".
   correct approach: Push in the order prev, ear, next, capturing prev and next BEFORE the ear test, and push all three before calling remove_node.
3. Advancing with `ear = ear.next` after a successful clip instead of `ear = next.next`, or updating `ear` but forgetting `stop = next.next`.
   diverges because: The "skip the next vertex" heuristic is what produces the observed every-other-vertex pattern (n=2: 4-5-0, 0-1-2, 2-3-4, 4-0-2). Without the skip you get the fan-like sequence instead. Forgetting to also reset `stop` leaves a stale sentinel, so the `ear == stop` fallback can trigger spuriously mid-run and inject cureLocalIntersections/splitEarcut triangles.
   correct approach: After remove_node(ear), execute BOTH `ear = arena[next].next` and `stop = arena[next].next`, then `continue` to re-test the while condition. Assert indices.len() == 3*(N-2) during development — any shortfall or surplus means the skip or the stop reset is wrong.
4. Using `> 0.0` instead of `>= 0.0` in the ear reflex test `if area(a,b,c) >= 0 return false`.
   diverges because: With `> 0.0`, exactly-collinear vertices (area == 0) are accepted as ears and emit degenerate triangles that the oracle never emits. With `< 0.0` written as `<= 0.0` on the accept side, the same. This is the single most output-sensitive comparison in the library.
   correct approach: A vertex is a candidate ear only when area(prev, ear, next) is STRICTLY negative; the guard is written as an early-out `if area(a,b,c) >= 0.0 { return false }` in both is_ear and is_ear_hashed.
5. Making point_in_triangle exclusive (`> 0.0`) or reordering its three cross products.
   diverges because: All three tests are inclusive `>= 0.0`, so a candidate lying exactly on an ear edge or at a vertex counts as inside and vetoes the ear. Switching to strict would accept ears the oracle rejects on degenerate input; and the ear node itself relies on the inclusive form to be caught by the first clause and then rejected by the area clause.
   correct approach: Copy the three expressions verbatim: (cx-px)*(ay-py)-(ax-px)*(cy-py) >= 0 && (ax-px)*(by-py)-(bx-px)*(ay-py) >= 0 && (bx-px)*(cy-py)-(cx-px)*(by-py) >= 0.
6. Clearing prev/next (or removing the arena entry) inside remove_node.
   diverges because: filterPoints does `remove_node(p); p = p.prev;` and cureLocalIntersections does `remove_node(p); remove_node(p.next);` — both read the STALE links of a node that was just unlinked. Zeroing them to NIL panics on index usize::MAX or silently walks the wrong ring. Removing from the Vec invalidates every other NodeId.
   correct approach: remove_node only writes the NEIGHBOURS' links (and patches the z chain). The removed node keeps its own prev/next untouched forever, and the arena is strictly append-only — never Vec::remove, never swap_remove, never shrink.
7. Reaching for Rc<RefCell<Node>> or raw pointers to model the doubly-linked list.
   diverges because: Rc cycles leak and RefCell double-borrows panic exactly where the algorithm mutates a node while walking from it (e.g. splitPolygon rewires four nodes at once, one of which may be aliased). Raw pointers reintroduce the unsafety the port is meant to avoid.
   correct approach: A single Vec<Node> arena with usize handles and NIL = usize::MAX. Expose copy accessors (x, y, pv, nx, zz) and mutate via one-line `self.arena[id].field = v` statements; never hold a &mut Node across another &mut self call.
8. Getting the winding sum wrong: swapping the operands to (prev.x - cur.x) * (cur.y + prev.y), or testing `sum >= 0` / `clockwise != (sum > 0)`.
   diverges because: The sign of `sum` decides forward versus reverse insertion, which decides both the ring traversal direction and which vertex is returned as the start node. Flipping it turns the CCW unit-circle ring into a reversed ring, so the first triangle becomes (1, 0, N-1) and every index in the output changes.
   correct approach: With j = i-1 (wrapping, initialised to len-1): sum += (points[j].x - points[i].x) * (points[i].y + points[j].y). Insert FORWARD iff `clockwise == (sum > 0.0)` with a strict `>`. For this test sum > 0 and clockwise = true, so insertion is forward and the returned node is N-1.
9. Assuming linkedList always returns the highest index, and mishandling the reverse branch.
   diverges because: The reverse loop inserts N-1, N-2, ..., 0, so the last inserted node — and hence the returned start node — is vertex 0, and the ring traverses in DECREASING index order. Code that hardcodes N-1 as the start node breaks for clockwise input rings and for every hole (holes are built with clockwise=false).
   correct approach: Always return the `last` variable from whichever loop ran. Never compute the start node from N.
10. Getting the hashing gate off by one, or testing it against the wrong variable.
   diverges because: threshold starts at 80 and has each ring's point count subtracted; hashing = (threshold < 0), i.e. total points > 80 strictly. N=80 (n=26, threshold 0) must NOT hash; N=81 (n=27, threshold -1) must hash. Also `len` is accumulated only inside the `threshold >= 0` guard, so with many rings len is a short count and must not be reused as the gate.
   correct approach: Loop `while threshold >= 0 && i < polygon.len()`, subtract into threshold, then set hashing = threshold < 0. Note that for THIS test a wrong gate is invisible (both paths emit the same triangles), so it will not be caught by difftest — get it right by construction.

   diverges because: The prevZ walk continues while `z >= minZ` and the nextZ walk while `z <= maxZ`, both inclusive; making either strict skips legitimate blocking vertices and accepts non-ears. The exclusions are `p != ear.prev && p != ear.next` only — omitting them lets a reflex neighbour a or c veto the ear (point_in_triangle is inclusive so a and c always test as inside).
   correct approach: Loop 1: `p != NIL && z[p] >= minZ && n != NIL && z[n] <= maxZ`, checking p, advancing p, checking n, advancing n. Loop 2: `p != NIL && z[p] >= minZ`. Loop 3: `n != NIL && z[n] <= maxZ`. Exclude only a and c; do NOT add a `p != ear` check (unnecessary — ear self-rejects via its own area test — and both walks start from ear.prevZ/ear.nextZ anyway).
12. Writing sortLinked's merge comparison as `z[p] < z[q]` instead of `z[p] <= z[q]`, or exiting on the wrong condition.
   diverges because: `<=` makes the merge stable. Equal-z nodes are common (the Morton grid is only 15 bits per axis, so nearby circle points collide), and an unstable merge permutes their prevZ/nextZ neighbours, changing the isEarHashed scan order. Exiting on `num_merges < 1`, or before `tail.nextZ = NIL`, corrupts or truncates the chain.
   correct approach: Four-way branch in order: p_size==0 -> take q; q_size==0 || q==NIL -> take p; z[p] <= z[q] -> take p; else take q. Terminate with `if num_merges <= 1 { return list }` tested after the pass, and null-terminate via tail (guarding tail != NIL, since the C++ dereferences it unconditionally).
13. Mis-transcribing sortLinked's run-measurement loop or the inner while condition.
   diverges because: The measure loop increments p_size BEFORE advancing q and breaks when q becomes NIL, so p_size counts the node just stepped off of. Restructuring it as advance-then-count under-counts the first run by one and drops nodes from the sorted chain. The inner condition `p_size > 0 || (q_size > 0 && q != NIL)` must keep the `q != NIL` conjunct inside the second disjunct only.
   correct approach: Transcribe verbatim: `for _ in 0..in_size { p_size += 1; q = next_z(q); if q == NIL { break } }`, then `q_size = in_size`, then `while p_size > 0 || (q_size > 0 && q != NIL)`.
14. "Improving" indexCurve by storing sortLinked's return value, or recomputing z unconditionally.
   diverges because: The sorted head is intentionally discarded — isEarHashed only ever walks outward from `ear` via prevZ/nextZ, so no head is needed and keeping one invites stale-pointer bugs after removals. Recomputing z on every indexCurve pass is harmless for coordinates but breaks the memoisation contract that split_polygon's fresh nodes (z == 0) rely on being distinguishable.
   correct approach: `if z == 0 { z = z_order(x, y) }`, seed prevZ/nextZ from prev/next, then cut the circle open (`p.prevZ.nextZ = NIL; p.prevZ = NIL` with p == start) and call sort_linked(p) discarding the result. indexCurve runs on every earcut_linked call with pass == 0, including split_earcut's two sub-ring calls.
15. Computing the hashing bbox from the raw ring 0 coordinate array instead of walking the linked list from outerNode.
   diverges because: earcut.hpp walks the list AFTER eliminateHoles, so the bbox includes hole vertices; earcut.js scans only the outer ring's raw data. These genuinely differ once holes exist, which shifts every z value and hence the isEarHashed scan order. For this single-ring test they coincide, so the bug hides.
   correct approach: Seed min/max from outerNode's own coordinates, then walk p = outerNode.next until p == outerNode. Then invSize = max(maxX-minX, maxY-minY) and invSize = if invSize != 0.0 { 32767.0/invSize } else { 0.0 } — note the `!= 0.0` guard, not an epsilon.
16. Rewriting the atoi edge cases with Rust's str::parse.
   diverges because: parse::<i32>() rejects any trailing garbage and any leading whitespace, so "3x", "1e3" and "3.9" fall through to the default and print nothing while the oracle prints the n=3, n=1 and n=3 triangulations. This was measured: a prototype with naive parsing scored exactly 67/70 with those three as the only failures. parse also rejects "2147483648" where atoi yields -2147483648.
   correct approach: Hand-roll glibc semantics: skip C-isspace, optional single sign, greedily consume ASCII digits, return 0 if no digits, accumulate in i64 saturating to i64::MIN/MAX on overflow, then truncate to i32 with `as i32`. Verify against the confirmed table ("abc"->0, "3x"->3, "1e3"->1, "3.9"->3, "+5"->5, "  7"->7, "0x10"->0, "2147483648"->-2147483648, "4294967296"->0, "99999999999999"->276447231, "9223372036854775808"->-1).
17. Using a checked/panicking multiply for n*3, or treating a non-positive count as an error.
   diverges because: gcc emits a wrapping i32 multiply; `n * 3` in debug Rust panics on overflow (e.g. n = -2147483648 from "2147483648") and prints a backtrace to stderr with exit code 101 instead of producing empty stdout. Treating n <= 0 as an error, or indexing polygon[0][0], panics on the one-empty-ring polygon.
   correct approach: m = n.wrapping_mul(3); loop `while i < m` so it runs zero times for m <= 0; build a polygon containing one EMPTY ring; let linked_list return NIL and let the top-level guard return with zero indices. Also make the capacity estimate `len*3/2 - polygon[0].len()/2` saturating (or omit it) so it cannot underflow.
18. Printing a trailing newline, separating with spaces instead of terminating with them, or exiting via std::process::exit.
   diverges because: The verified format is every index followed by exactly one 0x20, with no newline anywhere and zero bytes for an empty list — a join(" ") drops the final space and a println! adds a 0x0a, both single-byte md5 mismatches on all 70 cases. Rust's stdout is a LineWriter, so with no newline the tail sits in the buffer; std::process::exit skips the flush and silently truncates the output.
   correct approach: Build one String pushing `v.to_string()` then ' ' per index, write_all it, call flush() explicitly, and return normally from main. Verify with xxd that n=1 gives exactly 31 20 32 20 30 20.
19. Reimplementing cos/sin, changing the angle expression's grouping, or using a hand-written PI.
   diverges because: C evaluates ((2.0 * M_PI) * (double)i) / (double)(n*3); precomputing (2*PI/m) and multiplying by i gives different last bits. Different trig also gives different last bits, which perturbs the Morton codes and could in principle flip an exactly-zero area test.
   correct approach: Use std::f64::consts::PI (bit-identical to M_PI) and f64::cos/f64::sin (which link to the platform libm on Linux, matching the C++ binary), and write `2.0 * PI * (i as f64) / (m as f64)` so the grouping matches. Reassurance: because the output is combinatorially determined (every candidate is a valid ear, triangle count always N-2), 1-ulp differences cannot change the emitted indices for this input family — but do not rely on that for the general port.
20. Resetting `pass` incorrectly in the fallback chain, or calling the wrong cleanup function per pass.
   diverges because: The chain is exact: pass 0 exhaustion -> earcutLinked(filterPoints(ear), 1); pass 1 -> earcutLinked(cureLocalIntersections(filterPoints(ear)), 2); pass 2 -> splitEarcut(ear), which itself calls earcutLinked(a, 0) and earcutLinked(c, 0) with pass reset to 0 so indexCurve re-runs on each half. Getting this wrong emits extra or missing triangles on self-intersecting input. It never fires for this test (triangle count is always N-2), so difftest cannot catch it.
   correct approach: Transcribe the three-branch if/else-if on `pass` verbatim, always followed by `break`, and pass literal 0 in splitEarcut's two recursive calls. Temporarily eprintln! in the fallback branch to confirm it never fires for n in 0..2000.
21. Comparing NodeIds where the C++ compares .i, or vice versa.
   diverges because: splitPolygon mints two brand-new nodes that duplicate an existing node's i/x/y. intersectsPolygon, isValidDiagonal and splitEarcut deliberately compare `.i` so those clones are treated as the same vertex, while isEarHashed and the ear loop compare node identity. Swapping either way makes diagonal validation accept self-intersecting cuts.
   correct approach: Use `.i` comparisons in isValidDiagonal (a.next.i != b.i, a.prev.i != b.i), intersectsPolygon (all four), and splitEarcut (a.i != b.i); use handle equality in isEarHashed (p != a, p != c) and in every `p != start` ring-walk terminator.

   diverges because: Bare rustc defaults to edition 2015 while Cargo builds edition 2021, and the deliverable must satisfy both. Edition-sensitive constructs then compile one way and fail (or behave differently) the other — notably array `.into_iter()` yielding references in 2015/2018 but values in 2021, and TryFrom/TryInto not being in the 2015 prelude.

================================================================================
PART 1 -- c_atoi: faithful pure-std reimplementation of glibc atoi
================================================================================

Contract (verified identical to glibc atoi on 73/73 vectors):
    glibc:  atoi(s)  ==  (int32_t)strtol(s, NULL, 10)
    where strtol saturates the *64-bit* result to i64::MIN / i64::MAX on overflow,
    and the cast to int32_t is a plain low-32-bits (wrapping) truncation.
    The sign is applied at 64-BIT WIDTH, BEFORE the 32-bit truncation. This ordering is
    essential and is what makes e.g. "-9223372036854775807" -> +1.

FUNCTION c_isspace(b : u8) -> bool:
    # C isspace() in the "C" locale, which is the only locale in play because the
    # program never calls setlocale(). EXACTLY six bytes, note 0x0B is included.
    RETURN b IN { 0x20 /* space */, 0x09 /* \t */, 0x0A /* \n */,
                  0x0B /* \v */,    0x0C /* \f */, 0x0D /* \r */ }
    # Implementation hint: a `matches!(b, b' ' | b'\t' | b'\n' | 0x0b | 0x0c | b'\r')` pattern.
    # DO NOT call u8::is_ascii_whitespace() (omits 0x0B) or char::is_whitespace() (adds
    # U+0085/U+00A0/U+2000..). See Pitfalls P2 and P3.

FUNCTION c_atoi(s : &[u8]) -> i32:
    i        : usize = 0
    # --- phase 1: skip leading C-locale whitespace ---
    WHILE i < len(s) AND c_isspace(s[i]):
        i += 1
    # --- phase 2: at most one optional sign ---
    neg : bool = false
    IF i < len(s) AND (s[i] == '+' OR s[i] == '-'):
        neg = (s[i] == '-')
        i += 1
    # --- phase 3: greedily consume ASCII decimal digits, accumulate in i64 with saturation ---
    acc : i64  = 0
    sat : bool = false            # sticky "we overflowed i64" flag
    WHILE i < len(s) AND is_ascii_digit(s[i]):        # only b'0'..=b'9'; bytes >=0x80 are NOT digits
        IF NOT sat:
            d : i64 = (s[i] - '0')
            # checked 64-bit accumulate; on the first overflow latch `sat` and stop accumulating,
            # but KEEP CONSUMING digits so that `i` still lands past the numeral (harmless here
            # because we discard the end pointer, but it keeps the loop structure obviously correct)
            IF checked_mul(acc,10) overflows OR checked_add(acc*10, d) overflows:
                sat = true
            ELSE:
                acc = acc*10 + d
        i += 1
    # --- phase 4: apply sign at 64-bit width, saturating ---
    v : i64
    IF sat:
        v = IF neg THEN i64::MIN ELSE i64::MAX      # exactly what strtol reports (with ERANGE)
    ELSE IF neg:
        v = wrapping_neg(acc)                       # acc is in [0, i64::MAX], so plain negation;
                                                    # wrapping_neg is defensive only
    ELSE:
        v = acc
    # --- phase 5: truncate to 32 bits, wrapping (this is the (int) cast in atoi) ---
    RETURN low_32_bits_as_signed(v)                 # Rust: `v as i32`  (defined wrapping truncation)

PROOF that "saturate to i64 then truncate" is exhaustively correct even though we accumulate the
magnitude positively:
  - positive numeral with magnitude > i64::MAX  -> glibc strtol saturates to i64::MAX. We set sat,
    neg=false, v=i64::MAX. Match.
  - negative numeral with magnitude > i64::MAX  -> the true value is < i64::MIN, so glibc saturates
    to i64::MIN. We set sat, neg=true, v=i64::MIN. Match.
  - negative numeral with magnitude EXACTLY 2^63 ("-9223372036854775808") -> representable, glibc
    returns i64::MIN with errno==0. Our positive accumulation overflows, sets sat, and we emit
    i64::MIN anyway. Same VALUE (we simply don't model errno, which the program never reads). Match.
  - everything else fits and is exact.

PART 2 -- ARGV HANDLING: argc>1 detection, default, extras, non-UTF8
================================================================================

C side:
    int n = 1;
    if (argc > 1) n = std::atoi(argv[1]);
    // argv[2..] never read. argv[0] never read.

Rust side -- the ONLY correct formulation:

FUNCTION parse_n() -> i32:
    MATCH std::env::args_os().nth(1):          # nth(1) skips argv[0]; None <=> argc == 1
        None       => RETURN 1                 # the `int n = 1` default
        Some(osstr) => RETURN c_atoi( raw_bytes_of(osstr) )

Mapping of C concepts to Rust:
  * `argc > 1`            <=> `std::env::args_os().nth(1).is_some()`.
    Equivalent but worse: `std::env::args_os().count() > 1`. Prefer `nth(1)` -- it is a single
    fused lookup, expresses "read argv[1]" directly, and avoids walking the whole vector.
  * `argv[1]`             <=> the `OsString` yielded by `nth(1)`.
  * `argv[2], argv[3], ...` are IGNORED simply by never asking for them. There is no argument
    validation, no "too many arguments" error, no usage message. VERIFIED: the oracle produces
    byte-identical output for `2`, `2 junk`, and `2 junk extra`.
  * `argv[0]` is never inspected; the program's behaviour does not depend on its own name.

raw_bytes_of(osstr) -- two acceptable strategies, both verified byte-identical to the oracle:

  STRATEGY A (preferred on Linux; zero-copy, exactly the kernel's bytes):
      use std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt;      // brings `as_bytes()` into scope
      raw_bytes_of(os) = os.as_os_str().as_bytes()      // -> &[u8], never fails
    This is the true analogue of C's `char*`. It is unix-only. If the deliverable must also
    typecheck on non-unix hosts, gate it:
      #[cfg(unix)]     use OsStrExt::as_bytes
      #[cfg(not(unix))] fall back to STRATEGY B

  STRATEGY B (portable fallback, provably equivalent FOR THIS GRAMMAR):
      let s = osstr.to_string_lossy();  raw_bytes_of = s.as_bytes()
    Lossy conversion replaces each invalid byte/sequence with U+FFFD (bytes EF BF BD). This is
    SAFE here because U+FFFD's bytes are all >= 0x80, and 0x80..=0xFF is never a c_isspace byte,
    never '+'/'-', and never an ASCII digit. So a replacement character terminates the numeral in
    exactly the same place the original invalid byte would have. Verified: "5\xff" -> 5 and
    "\xff5" -> 0 under both strategies, matching the oracle.

  FORBIDDEN: `std::env::args()`. See Pitfall P4 -- it PANICS on non-UTF8 argv, and the oracle

PART 4 -- REPRODUCING `angle = 2.0 * M_PI * i / (n * 3)` BIT-FOR-BIT
================================================================================

C expression, fully parenthesized per C's left-to-right associativity for `*` and `/`
(they share precedence, so the expression is a left-leaning chain):
        angle = ( ( 2.0 * M_PI ) * (double)i ) / (double)(n * 3)
  - `2.0 * M_PI` is a compile-time constant fold of two doubles.
  - `i` is `int`, promoted to `double` by the usual arithmetic conversions.
  - `n * 3` is computed ENTIRELY IN int (wrapping, per Part 3) and THEN promoted to double.

Rust expression -- write it in exactly this shape:
        let angle: f64 = 2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI * (i as f64) / (total as f64);
  Rust's `*` and `/` are also same-precedence left-associative, so this parses as
        (( 2.0 * PI ) * (i as f64)) / (total as f64)
  which is the identical evaluation tree. Three floating-point operations, in this order:
        t1 = 2.0 * PI            (exact: see below)
        t2 = t1 * (double)i      (one IEEE-754 round-to-nearest-even)
        angle = t2 / (double)total (one IEEE-754 round-to-nearest-even)

Constant identity -- VERIFIED by dumping raw bit patterns from both languages:
        C   M_PI                     = 0x400921FB54442D18
        Rust std::f64::consts::PI    = 0x400921FB54442D18     <- IDENTICAL
        C   2.0 * M_PI               = 0x401921FB54442D18
        Rust 2.0 * PI                = 0x401921FB54442D18     <- IDENTICAL
  `2.0 * PI` is EXACT (multiplying by 2 only increments the exponent; the 52-bit significand is
  untouched), so there is no rounding difference from folding it at compile time vs. at run time.
  M_PI in glibc's <math.h> is the `double` literal 3.14159265358979323846; the digits round to the
  same bit pattern as Rust's PI. Never hand-write a decimal literal for pi -- use the std constant.

Int-to-double conversion:
  - `(double)i` for i in 0..total: total <= 2^31-1, and every i32 is exactly representable in f64
    (f64 has 53 significand bits > 32), so `i as f64` is EXACT and matches C's int->double.
  - `(double)(n*3)`: same, EXACT, and it converts the ALREADY-WRAPPED int. Vector #51 proves this:
    argv "1431655767" gives n*3 == 5 (wrapped), the divisor is 5, and the oracle emits a clean
    5-gon triangulation "3 4 0 0 1 2 2 3 0 ". Had the divisor been the mathematically-correct
    4294967301, all 5 points would collapse into a ~7e-10 arc and the output would differ.
  - Rust's `as f64` on i32 is a lossless, well-defined conversion (no UB, no saturation quirks).

Why f64::cos / f64::sin match glibc bit-for-bit on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu:
  1. Rust's `f64::cos`/`f64::sin` are thin wrappers over the LLVM intrinsics `llvm.cos.f64` /
     `llvm.sin.f64`, which LLVM lowers to CALLS INTO THE PLATFORM libm. There is no Rust-internal
     software implementation of cos/sin for this target.
  2. VERIFIED by inspecting the linked binary: a Rust program computing `angle.cos()` and
     `angle.sin()` yields the dynamic relocation
         R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT  sincos@GLIBC_2.2.5
     i.e. it imports the symbol from libm.so.6 -- the very same
     /opt/compiler/gcc-12/lib/libm.so.6 (glibc 2.33) that `ldd /workspace/dataset/test1_executable`
     shows the oracle linking. Same code, same rounding, same bits.
     (LLVM contracted the adjacent cos+sin pair into one `sincos` call. glibc's sincos is
     documented and verified to return exactly what separate cos/sin return, so this fusion is
     value-neutral -- confirmed by the bit dumps below.)
  3. Rust has NO fast-math / -ffast-math / -ffp-contract=fast equivalent. f64 arithmetic is strict
     IEEE-754 round-to-nearest-even at every optimization level. And the angle expression contains
     only `*` and `/` with no intervening `+`, so there is no FMA contraction opportunity for GCC
     to have taken on the C side either.
  4. EMPIRICAL PROOF (this is the real evidence, not the reasoning above): a C++ probe and a Rust
     probe each computed `angle`, `cos(angle)`, `sin(angle)` for every i over n in
     {1,2,3,5,27,80,81,100,333,1365,2000} (total point counts 3..6000), printed all three raw
     u64 bit patterns, and FNV-1a-hashed the whole stream. Every per-i triple and every per-n hash
     matched EXACTLY. Sample (n=3):
         i=1  angle=3FE657184AE74487  cos=3FE8836FA2CF5039  sin=3FE491B7523C161C
         i=4  angle=400657184AE74487  cos=BFEE11F642522D1B  sin=3FD5E3A8748A0BF8
         i=8  angle=401657184AE74487  cos=3FE8836FA2CF5037  sin=BFE491B7523C161F
     Full-stream hashes, C++ == Rust: n=3 -> 47269066E1F43AF3, n=81 -> 67FE47E7EC03C880,
     n=2000 -> 67FB1A9B90C79A97. Identical at Rust opt-level 0 AND 3.
     Note the deliberately "wrong-looking" values that MUST be reproduced, e.g. for n=1:
         cos(2pi/3) = BFDFFFFFFFFFFFFC  (not exactly -0.5)
         cos(4pi/3) = BFE0000000000004
     and for n=2: sin(pi) = 3CA1A62633145C07 (~1.2246e-16, not 0). These tiny residuals feed
     directly into earcut's `area()` sign tests, so they are not cosmetic.

FUNCTION build_ring(total : i32) -> Vec<[f64;2]>:
    ring = empty vector                       # C: std::vector, default-constructed, no reserve
    i : i32 = 0
    WHILE i < total:
        angle : f64 = 2.0 * PI * (i as f64) / (total as f64)   # recomputed FROM SCRATCH each i
        ring.push( [ cos(angle), sin(angle) ] )                # x = cos, y = sin, in THIS order
        i += 1
    RETURN ring
  * Recompute `angle` from `i` every iteration. Do NOT hoist `2.0*PI/total` into a step and
    accumulate or multiply -- that changes the rounding sequence. See Pitfall P11/P12.
  * `Vec::with_capacity(total as usize)` is a safe, purely-allocative optimisation ONLY when
    total > 0; it does not affect the values. Guard the cast.

PART 5 -- OUTPUT: byte-exact, buffered, flushed
================================================================================

C:  for (auto idx : indices) std::cout << idx << " ";
    - `indices` is std::vector<uint32_t>; `idx` is uint32_t.
    - `operator<<(ostream&, unsigned int)` in the default (classic "C") locale: plain decimal,
      no sign, no zero padding, no field width, NO THOUSANDS SEPARATOR (numpunct<char>::grouping
      is empty). VERIFIED: the n=2000 output contains "5999", never "5,999"; grep for ',' finds 0.
    - Each index is followed by EXACTLY ONE 0x20 space, INCLUDING THE LAST ONE.
      VERIFIED: n=1 stdout is exactly 6 bytes `31 20 32 20 30 20` = "1 2 0 ".
      VERIFIED: the final byte of the n=2000 output is 0x20; there is NO 0x0A anywhere.
    - Empty `indices` => zero bytes written.
    - Nothing else is ever written; stderr is empty; exit status 0.

Rust, byte-exact equivalent:  per element, emit `format!("{} ", v)` for v: u32 -- i.e. Rust's
`Display for u32` (identical decimal digits, no separators, no sign) followed by one b' '.
NO `println!`, NO trailing newline, NO separator-joining (`join(" ")` would drop the final space).

Fast + exact writer (this is the shape to ship):

FUNCTION write_indices(idx : &[u32]) -> io::Result<()>:
    use std::io::Write
    stdout_handle = std::io::stdout()
    # Lock ONCE for the whole run, and wrap the lock in a BufWriter.
    # - locking once removes a mutex acquire per element
    # - BufWriter coalesces into 64 KiB write(2) syscalls instead of one per element
    w = BufWriter::with_capacity(65536, stdout_handle.lock())
    scratch : [u8; 10] = uninit          # u32::MAX == 4294967295 is 10 digits; 10 bytes suffice
    FOR v IN idx:
        # manual reverse itoa -- avoids the fmt::Display machinery entirely
        p = 10
        x = v
        REPEAT:
            p -= 1
            scratch[p] = '0' + (x % 10)
            x /= 10
        UNTIL x == 0                     # do-while: guarantees at least one digit, so v==0 -> "0"
        w.write_all(&scratch[p..10])?    # the digits
        w.write_all(b" ")?               # the mandatory single trailing space
    w.flush()?                           # <-- MANDATORY. See Pitfall P18.
    RETURN Ok

Performance, MEASURED on 5,000,000 indices:
    per-element `print!("{} ", i)`                            201 ms   (per-call lock + LineWriter)
    BufWriter<StdoutLock> + `write!(w, "{} ", i)`               88 ms   (2.3x faster)
    BufWriter<StdoutLock> + manual itoa (the shape above)       60 ms   (3.3x faster)
All three produced BYTE-IDENTICAL output (verified by md5 at 20 and 100 elements). So the
optimisation is free: pick the fastest, it cannot change the bytes.
An equally valid variant: build the entire payload in one `Vec<u8>` (reserve idx.len()*11) and
issue a single `write_all` on the locked stdout. Same bytes, similar speed, more peak memory.

Flushing:
  * `BufWriter` flushes in its `Drop` impl, but Drop SWALLOWS the error -- so on a short write you
    would silently truncate. Call `.flush()` explicitly and let the caller see the Result.
  * Rust's `stdout()` is a `LineWriter`; because this program emits NO newlines, nothing is ever
    auto-flushed by the line-buffering heuristic. Data sits in the buffer until an explicit flush,
    a full buffer, or std's end-of-main cleanup. Do not rely on the cleanup: it does not run under
    `std::process::exit()` and is not contractually guaranteed. Flush explicitly.
  * Return the io::Result to `main` and DISCARD it (`let _ = ...`). Do not unwrap. See P19.
